notes:
Random experiment and sample space

  • A random experiment has more than one possible outcome and the outcome cannot be predicted with certainty. The set of all possible outcomes is the sample space $S$.
  • An event is any subset of $S$. The sure event is $S$ itself; the impossible event is $\emptyset$.

Common sample spaces

Experiment$n(S)$
One die thrown6
Two dice thrown36
A coin tossed $n$ times$2^n$
One card from a deck52 (4 suits $\times$ 13, 4 aces, 12 face cards)

Axiomatic (Kolmogorov) approach

  • $0 \le P(A) \le 1$ for every event $A$; $P(S)=1$; $P(\emptyset)=0$.
  • If $A,B$ are mutually exclusive (cannot occur together), $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$.
  • For equally likely outcomes: $P(A)=\dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)}$ = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.

Algebra of events

  • Complement: $P(A')=1-P(A)$.
  • Addition theorem (general): $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$.
  • If $A,B$ are mutually exclusive, $P(A\cap B)=0$, so the theorem reduces to $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)$.
  • Events are exhaustive if their union is the whole sample space $S$. If $A,B$ are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive, $P(A)+P(B)=1$.

Odds

  • If odds in favour of an event are $a:b$, then $P(\text{event})=\dfrac{a}{a+b}$; odds against are $b:a$.

Exam tip

KCET typically sets 2-3 questions from this chapter, mostly classic dice/coin/card probability calculations and one on the addition theorem or mutually exclusive/exhaustive events. Always double check $n(S)$ (36 for two dice, $2^n$ for $n$ coins, 52 for cards) before counting favourable outcomes.
